title: Cap all political donations, not only those from overseas, Burnham told
summary:
Experts say ‘insanely complex’ £100,000 limit proposed for overseas donors should be replaced by universal cap

Andy Burnham is facing calls to commit to a cap on all political donations when…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is facing calls to commit to a cap on all political donations when the elections bill is in the House of Lords, instead of the “insanely complex” £100,000 limit on overseas donors. It is uncertain whether the £72m worth of donations recently received by Reform UK will be affected.

The Labour former home secretary David Blunkett is one of many peers to have tabled an amendment calling for an overall cap, proposing a £500,000 annual limit per donor, with his plan believed to have broad support.

Various amendments to the legislation, known officially as the representation of the people bill, are due to be debated in the House of Lords in the coming weeks, with proposals for a cap set at levels ranging from £1,000 to £5m a year.

No 10 has previously promised to bring forward a taskforce that will look at the possibility of a wider donations cap as part of tackling mega-donations. However, sources say senior figures would prefer this to be brought forward in a new bill aimed at cleaning up politics in the next session of parliament, rather than holding up current legislation. Labour is also yet to overcome the opposition of unions worried that limits affecting their own ability to donate could water down their influence.

Before the Lords debate, experts are urging the government to replace the overseas cap with a blanket cap for all donors to avoid the numerous possible loopholes in the new law applying to donors based abroad.

The overseas donor cap was announced in March and is meant to apply from that point, meaning it could cover Reform’s £36m from the crypto billionaire Ben Delo and a further £36m from Christopher Harborne donated this autumn.
However, Reform insists it will not have to hand back the money and will challenge the law’s retrospective application in the courts, given it has not yet passed.

Delo’s donation is less likely to be caught by the cap as he has long been registered to vote in the UK, but Harborne’s donation is more in contention because he has previously been an overseas elector and registered to vote in Britain only in June this year.

blocks.caption: Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK. The party has said it will challenge any retrospective application of the elections bill in the courts.  Photograph: Peter Nicholls/Getty Images

blocks.text: Some officials are worried about the prospect of a judicial review in relation to the retrospective aspect of the legislation, with the House of Lords constitution committee saying it “has not been sufficiently justified and would set an unwelcome precedent”.

However, government sources insist this element will go ahead, saying retrospective legislation is not a new concept and there are multiple precedents under successive administrations, particularly to address the risk of people taking action immediately to avoid the new rules.

New government amendments to the elections bill, aimed at tightening the overseas donor cap, bring in complicated rules around donations held in trusts and as loans, as well as requiring formal declarations about residency aimed at identifying which donations may have to be returned.
But Rose Zussman, a senior policy manager at Transparency International UK, said: “If a cap is right for donors living overseas, it’s right for all donors.”

She added: “These amendments concede that unlimited donations put our democracy at risk, but stop short of the obvious solution. Singling out one group of donors risks appearing partisan and makes already complex rules harder to follow. The simpler answer, and one the public overwhelmingly backs, is a universal cap on how much anyone can give to a political party.”

Susan Hawley, the director of Spotlight on Corruption, agreed that an overall donations cap would be simpler. “With almost 180 government amendments, this bill is now becoming insanely complex, which will make it extremely hard to navigate and enforce,” she said.

“But it is also clear that the government is disregarding the mood of the country by sticking its head in the sand instead of taking steps to get big money and undue influence out of party political funding, by introducing a donation cap and spending limits.”
Stella Creasy, the Labour MP who proposed a £100,000 cap when the bill was in the Commons, said a separate piece of legislation for a cap would be too late.

blocks.caption: Stella Creasy, the Labour MP who proposed the £100,000 limit on overseas donations. Photograph: PjrNews/Alamy

blocks.text: “If you are concerned about billionaires buying the next election, you have to stop it at the source,” she said. “You can’t wait until it’s been spent and then say that was too much. I have been taken aback at the strength of feeling in the House of Lords that we cannot let billionaires with UK postcodes define the next election.”

Despite Burnham’s previous support for a donation cap, trade unions have been pushing back against the idea over fears that a rightwing government could take steps to stop large donations from their movement in future.

Shaun Bowler, the founder of the grassroots campaign WakeUpGB, who previously secured written support for a cap from Burnham before he became prime minister, said: “I approached Andy Burnham in good faith and welcomed his support for a donation cap. I genuinely believed he wanted to change the culture of Westminster.

“But when his government subsequently declined to back a general cap, I felt he had broken the pledge he made to me. Now parliament has a £1,000 proposal before it. I welcome that, but why should trade unions be exempt?

“Unions historically helped Labour counter wealthy Conservative donors. I understand that. But the answer isn’t to preserve enormous donations on either side. It is to introduce the same fair limit for everyone.”
